subject: Banking
title: Financial System Stability
description: A quick, practical guide to Financial System Stability.

hook.text: In March 2020, financial markets froze. The Fed stepped in within days, lending $2 trillion to keep the system alive.

buildup.text: Central banks monitor systemic risk. They watch for signs that a failing bank or market could trigger wider collapse.

discovery.text: Stress tests simulate crises before they happen. Banks must prove they can survive a severe recession to keep operating.

twist.text: Markets expect central bank rescues. The 'Fed put' encourages risk-taking because traders assume a safety net exists.

climax.text: Stability is the central bank's unwritten mandate. Markets function only because everyone believes the backstop exists.

punchline.text: $2 trillion in days. Central banks keep the financial system breathing.

quiz.question: What is the 'Fed put'?
options: The market expectation that the Fed will rescue markets in a crisis

details.summary: Central banks monitor and protect financial system stability by supervising banks, acting as lenders of last resort during panics, and developing macroprudential tools to prevent risks from spreading across institutions.
details.whyItMatters: A stable financial system underpins the entire economy. When it fails, as in 2008, the consequences cascade rapidly into unemployment, lost savings, and recessions that affect everyone.
takeaways: Macroprudential regulation focuses on system-wide risks, not just individual banks
Central banks run stress tests to identify vulnerable institutions
The lender of last resort function prevents bank runs from spreading

faq.question: How do central banks prevent financial crises?
faq.answer: They monitor interconnections between banks, set capital and liquidity requirements, run stress tests, and intervene early when institutions show signs of distress. They also manage panics by providing emergency liquidity.

faq.question: What is macroprudential regulation?
faq.answer: Unlike traditional regulation that looks at individual bank safety, macroprudential policy watches for risks building across the entire financial system. Tools include countercyclical capital buffers that force banks to build reserves during booms.
